resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] GROUP BY, HAVING or an aggregate over many rows. DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads (Select = COUNT), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query).

migration_waves.title: Move to Aurora MySQL
migration_waves.rationale: The whole source database (MySQL 8.0.45) moves 1:1 to Aurora MySQL: same engine family. The collector reports engine and version only; feature compatibility is not assessed here. 70 queries (65.4%) remain on Aurora MySQL once later waves have moved their share; later waves move subsets of these 50 tables and views out of Aurora MySQL.
migration_waves.gate: Schema and data parity validated against the source database before cutover; decommission the legacy source once replication lag is zero.

migration_waves.title: Cache hot reads with ElastiCache
migration_waves.rationale: 20 hot reads (83.4% of calls), cache-aside in front of Aurora MySQL in wave 2, then DynamoDB once wave 3 moves these reads: no data migration, fully reversible. It takes the read pressure off before the data migrations that follow. These reads belong to queries that move in wave 1 (Aurora MySQL) and wave 3 (DynamoDB); this share overlaps the owner shares, which alone sum to 100%.
migration_waves.gate: Cache hit rate and invalidation verified against Aurora MySQL.

migration_waves.title: Move key-value and point-lookup queries to DynamoDB
migration_waves.rationale: 37 key-value and point-lookup queries (34.6% of query patterns) across 1 table group, respecting co-dependent tables where possible: the pattern DynamoDB fits best, and the smallest-blast-radius data migration available once the cache wave has absorbed the read pressure.
migration_waves.gate: Dual-write/backfill validated and query parity confirmed per table group. 3 tables (wordpress.wp_options, wordpress.wp_termmeta, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_api_keys) stay dual-read by Aurora MySQL queries, which remain on Aurora MySQL; DynamoDB owns them, so keep the Aurora MySQL copy in sync from DynamoDB via CDC. 24 queries read 15 tables (wordpress.wp_actionscheduler_actions, wordpress.wp_actionscheduler_groups, wordpress.wp_actionscheduler_logs, wordpress.wp_comments, wordpress.wp_postmeta, wordpress.wp_posts, wordpress.wp_term_relationships, wordpress.wp_term_taxonomy, wordpress.wp_terms, wordpress.wp_usermeta, wordpress.wp_users, wordpress.wp_wc_reserved_stock, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_order_itemmeta, wordpress.wp_woocommerce_order_items) Aurora MySQL owns (wave 1) and keeps owning; keep a DynamoDB copy of them in sync via CDC.

architectural_patterns.name: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)
architectural_patterns.description: Separate write operations (commands) from read operations (queries) across different databases. The write database is optimized for transactional consistency, while the read database is optimized for query performance and flexibility.
architectural_patterns.when: One engine handles most writes and another handles reads/search/analytics
architectural_patterns.example: DynamoDB handles all CRUD operations (writes + simple reads). OpenSearch serves as a read-optimized view for full-text search, faceted filtering, and analytics queries. Data flows from DynamoDB to OpenSearch via zero-ETL integration.

architectural_patterns.name: Event-Driven Sync
architectural_patterns.description: Use database change streams or event logs to propagate changes between databases asynchronously. Each database maintains its own optimized representation of the data.
architectural_patterns.when: Multiple engines need the same data in different shapes
architectural_patterns.example: DynamoDB Streams captures all item changes. A Lambda function transforms and routes changes to OpenSearch (for search) and ElastiCache (for leaderboards). Each consumer shapes the data for its specific access patterns.
